entries.title: The Painter Who Shaped Rothko
entries.summary: The usual story is that Milton Avery mentored, then was eclipsed by, the famed abstract expressionist. But it was more complicated than that.
entries.content:
The usual story is that Milton Avery mentored, then was eclipsed by, the famed abstract expressionist. But it was more complicated than that.

The evolution of European modern art can be explained as a story of susceptible young people falling under others’ spells and then asking, What can I do with this? How can I convert it to my purposes?

What’s remarkable is how often the main chapters of this story have unfolded in coastal or mountain retreats. Think of Claude Monet on the Normandy coast, wrestling with the influence of his mentor Eugène Boudin. Or Henri Matisse staying in Saint-Tropez with his mentor Paul Signac, before breaking with Signac’s neo-impressionist style and co-inventing fauvism. Or Pablo Picasso, goaded into radicalism by the latest bizarre creations of Matisse, retreating to the Spanish mountain village of Gósol and, mere months later, beginning work on his proto-cubist masterpiece, Les Demoiselles d’Avignon. All of these key episodes happened in agreeable resorts, seaside ports, and villages, far from the sophisticated cities assumed to have been the cauldrons of modernism.

Modern art in America is no different. Its story can scarcely be told without reference to artists summering on the Atlantic Coast, including Winslow Homer, Marsden Hartley, and Edward Hopper in Maine and Massachusetts and Jackson Pollock, Lee Krasner, and Willem de Kooning on Long Island.

Beginning in the early 1930s, three Americans—Milton Avery, Mark Rothko, and Adolph Gottlieb—began spending summers together on Cape Ann, along the coast of northeast Massachusetts. They loved the gritty authenticity of Gloucester, the nation’s oldest fishing port. Cape Ann’s distinctive, undulant geography combined pungent industry and village intensity with Atlantic immensity of sea and sky. The story of the relationships among these artists, in particular between the older Avery and the now–stratospherically famous Rothko, shows us American modernism in its moment of greatest transition.

Avery was the mentor figure, the one destined, in the usual telling of this story, to be eclipsed. Whereas Rothko is a regular subject of museum retrospectives in Europe and North America, and his paintings can sell at auction for as much as $98 million, Avery remains relatively unknown outside of the U.S. (The most expensive Avery sold at auction was a little more than $6 million, in 2022.) But are we telling the right story about Avery if we cast him in this role?

Certainly, when Rothko and Gottlieb, during World War II, turned to abstraction, they broke from Avery and, in short order, became central figures in a mid-century revolution—one that transformed modern art from a marginal activity to a cultural phenomenon attracting cash, prestige, and international acclaim. Avery wasn’t exactly forgotten in all of this, but he has long been overlooked.

He had first come to Gloucester in 1920, returning regularly during the summer until 1945. It’s where he met his wife, a fellow artist named Sally Michel. The fishing port was known as a bustling artists’ colony. In the 19th century, Homer and Fitz Henry Lane had spent productive time there, as had Hopper, Cecilia Beaux, and Stuart Davis in the 20th. So Avery was far from alone as he strolled around the harbor with his sketchbook and retired at night to rudimentary rooms lacking toilets and bathtubs. In 1932, he and Sally, who was pregnant with their only child, were joined on Cape Ann by Rothko—at the time called Markus Rothkowitz; he began using the name Mark Rothko in 1940—and Gottlieb.

Avery was in his element in Gloucester. Confident, good-humored, and in the noontime of life, he sat comfortably on his own shadow. Unlike his protégés, he was not especially intellectual. He was a taciturn pragmatist with a gentle sense of humor. He had a dog called Picasso. To those who said modern art was ugly and hard to appreciate, he would answer: “Olives taste ugly, too, until you learn to enjoy them.”

The two younger men felt his support, but he didn’t force his ideas on them. According to Eliza Rathbone, the curator of an exhibit about the trio’s seaside summers currently on view at the Cape Ann Museum, Avery “never uttered a word of advice or instruction to any painter other than ‘do another one.’” He set an example: how to be a modern artist, yes. But also: how to be a husband and father, how to carry on. His very reticence was liberating.

The three men had become friends in New York, where they would gather in the evenings to sketch and discuss art at the Averys’ Lincoln Square apartment. “I cannot tell you what it meant for us during those early years to be made welcome in those memorable studios,” Rothko would later recall.

In Gloucester, they explored the port, with its wharves and warehouses and fish-processing facilities, filling sketchbooks and painting small-scale works in watercolor. A total solar eclipse that August provided fodder for Avery, who made an amusing watercolor showing people on Good Harbor Beach looking at the celestial phenomenon through smoked glasses and colored film.

That first summer together was bookended by major life events back in New York. The Depression had flooded the streets with the unemployed. Gottlieb married in June. In October, as memories of summer receded, Sally gave birth to a daughter, and a few weeks later, Rothko married.

In those days, Rothko and Gottlieb would study Avery’s paintings and, according to Sally Avery, “take them apart.” On Cape Ann, they watched him treat the beach as a backdrop against which he placed monumental, thick-hipped figures, arranging areas of pattern (umbrellas, beachwear) against flat, colored shapes in compositions with shifting horizon lines. Following Avery’s example, they experimented with gouache and watercolor applied to colored construction paper.

The Averys and Gottliebs returned in the summer of 1933, and were joined by the Rothkos in 1934. The Depression was biting hard, but the artists’ life in Gloucester remained simple and uncorrupted. “We saw each other day in and day out,” Sally recalled of those years. “Evenings we’d gather to have a cup of tea and look at our day’s work. There was no talk of selling—only of painting.”

“I always thought Avery was a great artist,” Gottlieb would later say. “I always regarded him as a brilliant colorist and draftsman, a solitary figure working against the stream.” Gottlieb was right. Avery was one of the 20th century’s most original colorists. His expansive compositions were influenced by Pierre Bonnard and Matisse as well as by American folk art. Unlike Matisse, who loved bold, blatant colors, he favored unusual, in-between hues—mauves, browns, pale greens—all close in tonal value. He would often unify three or four slightly clashing varieties of the same color with a complementary hue elsewhere in the arrangement. Like spacious minor-key chords given a subtle major-key lift, these color combinations can arouse powerful emotions that are excruciatingly just short of fulfillment.

When it came to being influenced by others, Matisse understood what was at stake. But, he said, “I have never avoided the influence of others. I would have considered it cowardice and a lack of sincerity toward myself.”

To be open to influence is to risk being dislodged from your former self. It requires you to have the confidence to convert the ensuing upheaval to your own (still unknown) purposes. The process is complicated and rarely goes smoothly. Often, though not always, it involves some kind of betrayal.

No one betrays anyone in this story. All three artists remained friends. But the two younger painters, Rothko and Gottlieb, although deeply affected by Avery’s original way of painting, eventually decided that they needed to go further—to change not just the colors, the shapes, or the subjects, but something more fundamental.

In 1943, they broke away. Perhaps coincidentally, perhaps not, the breach happened just as Avery was beginning to thrive. He had been choosing larger canvases and distilling his paintings down to a few essential ingredients. The strategy was working. His work was selling. Dealers were fighting to represent him. He had a series of successful shows. The reviews were good.

Rothko, meanwhile, experienced a creative crisis and, in 1940, stopped painting for a year. He had been digging into philosophy, reading Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, and Kierkegaard, as well as the Greek myths and tragedies. Gottlieb, at the same time, made works merging surrealism with imagery inspired by masks and ritual objects from Africa, the Pacific, and Native North American cultures.

As the two younger men moved steadily closer to total abstraction, a tension that has in many ways defined American art—between the concreteness of the material world and the amorphousness of the sublime—was coming to a head. Avery, ever loyal to his sketchbook, remained committed to direct observation of particular people and places. His summer companions were about to throw in their lot with the sublime.

The push toward abstraction in mid-century American art coincided with a surge of interest in existentialism, which had begun to displace the pragmatism that underlay Avery’s approach. A sense that even the closest ties might be loosened by what T. S. Eliot—who had himself summered for nearly two decades in Gloucester—had described (in a review of James Joyce’s Ulysses) as an “immense panorama of futility and anarchy” was lent gravity by the world wars. But the human predicament, as Albert Camus made clear in The Stranger (1942), went beyond man-made conflict. It was inextricable from all that was inhuman, arbitrary, and immense—from the blinding energy of the sun on an Algerian beach, for instance.

On Cape Ann, Rothko and Gottlieb thought a lot about the sun, as well as the sea, the sky, and the smallness of human life. They were no doubt aware of the death-haunted history of Gloucester, where, between 1866 and 1890, more than 2,450 Gloucester men and 380 schooners failed to return from the fishing grounds. They wanted their art to communicate awe, and a sense of the insecurity and brutality of existence. It was as if the Atlantic were pulling them out to sea, away from both the harbor intimacy of Gloucester and the embrace of Milton and Sally Avery.

In 1943, Rothko and Gottlieb co-authored a letter and sent it to The New York Times, which published it on June 13. The letter responded to the Times critic Edward Alden Jewell, who, in a review, had misjudged (they felt) paintings by Rothko and Gottlieb. It also doubled as a five-point manifesto: “To us,” they wrote, “art is an adventure into an unknown world, which can be explored only by those willing to take risks.” That was the first point. The fourth point ended: “We are for flat forms because they destroy illusion and reveal truth.” According to the fifth point, “only that subject matter is valid which is tragic and timeless.” A concluding salvo declared that for their work to succeed, “it must insult anyone who is spiritually attuned to interior decoration; pictures of the home; pictures for over the mantle; pictures of the American scene”—the list continues—“prize-winning potboilers; the National Academy; the Whitney Academy,” and so on.

Avery could easily have felt personally targeted. He had exhibited, after all, at the first and second Whitney Biennials (in 1933 and 1936); he painted domestic interiors and American landscapes; and his pictures could be called “decorative” (at least in the sense Matisse meant when he described his more ambitious paintings as “decorations”).

He was probably too magnanimous—or phlegmatic—to take umbrage, and the summer proceeded pleasantly enough. If the group dynamic had become awkward, it correlated, the art historian Robert Hobbs wrote in his monograph of Avery, “with the way rebellions between initiates and their mentors are frequently enacted: certain brash rejections are cushioned with compliments, and personal assurances attempt to heal the break that has in actual fact been made.”

Which it had. Mentor and protégés went separate ways. They wouldn’t summer together again until 1957, when they reconvened in Provincetown on Cape Cod.

Sometimes after a clear-cut break, a reciprocity gradually reemerges. Even as the abstract expressionists transformed American art, Avery wasn’t entirely left behind. The period’s most influential critic, Clement Greenberg, cast Avery as a sort of John the Baptist to the artists whom Greenberg had tried to deify. The new crop of abstract painters, he wrote in 1957, “has certain salutary lessons to learn” from Avery “that they cannot learn from any other artist on the scene.”

In World War II’s immediate aftermath, Rothko painted abstract, colored shapes, beginning with what he called “multiforms” and shifting, around 1949, to his signature format of floating “lozenges” of soft-edged colors. He liked to layer warm and cool colors, so that in one lozenge a cooler purple might subdue a thin overlay of red while in its neighbor, a warm yellow rises like steam through the same red. The effect can be akin to music, and so intensely affecting that you’re almost willing to accept the artist’s preposterous rhetoric about his work. (“I would like to say to those who think of my pictures as serene,” Rothko once wrote, “that I have imprisoned the most utter violence in every inch of their surface.”)

Meanwhile, Avery, working now on larger canvases, let particulars of the observed world dissolve into trembling fields of color. The paintings remained recognizable depictions of sea, land, and sky, but they, too, had as their true subject something closer to music. A gallery in the Cape Ann Museum exhibit (which will travel to the Phillips Collection, in Washington, D.C., in October) allows these late Avery paintings to share space with a sequence of mature Rothkos and similarly spare Gottliebs. The sense the gallery creates is of all three artists tenderly reunited and singing together in unison.

If Rothko’s abstract paintings recall the ethereal, spatially ambiguous atmosphere of Caspar David Friedrich’s Monk by the Sea (painted between 1808 and 1810) or certain late works by J. M. W. Turner, they may also evoke the natural environment he observed on Cape Ann. His compositions are oriented vertically, but the lozenges nestled within each painting tend to be horizontal, so it’s tempting to see the thin strips dividing them as swaths of land hovering between sea and sky. Gottlieb, too, favored shapes that suggested the sun and moon—phenomena that he, a passionate sailor, had daily observed while out on the water.

Despite all of this concordance, I came away sensing something unresolved about the relationship among these three powerful artists. The late Averys are good, but they’re simply not as strong as the best Rothkos, which hum with colors so richly resonant that they make Avery’s attempts to work on a larger scale look anemic. The Averys also lack the deep, metaphysical suggestiveness of the Gottliebs.

Yet when you set aside the late works and consider Avery’s oeuvre, it seems to me that he was the better—more richly poetic, more generative—artist. The problem with the abstract expressionists’ relentless courting of the sublime was that the process of distillation produced too much bombast. And it led them into a cul-de-sac. As a skeptical character in John Updike’s novel Seek My Face put it, referring to the postwar generation of abstract expressionists, “they all still spoke of painting in terms of self-exploration and an agonized authenticity that would revolutionize the world and whatnot, but the results were a little like company logos, everybody working on the scale of 19th-century academic art but each of them having come up with some eye-catching simplification.”

After Rothko settled on his signature manner, the level of repetition in his work became oppressive. Gottlieb, too, as he chased the sublime, seemed to shun the finer tendrils of the sensuous world, with results that felt fatally monotonous.

To Greenberg, Avery was a prophet, his work a precursor to his younger peers’ more radical experiments. But maybe Avery was actually better than that. Rejecting Greenberg doesn’t mean claiming that abstraction was some kind of aesthetic mistake. But I would argue that, whereas Avery’s paintings continued to be aerated by the beautiful unruliness of the material world, Rothko and Gottlieb, especially later on, were relatively formulaic.

True, if forced to choose, I might prefer to look at my favorite single Rothko over my favorite single Avery. But I would rather spend time with a dozen of Avery’s finest works than a dozen of Rothko’s. That’s because Avery understood that a deep canyon separates things in the world from their representations in art. The mystery of painting lies in what takes place in that shadowy, fertile zone, where what you thought was green foliage turns into the strangest dark purple, that body of gray water has flushed vivid turquoise, the blue sky is now flaming orange, and you don’t even know whether these transformations have taken place in life or on the canvas.

Avery proved that figurative artists, in trying to represent the observable world, can be as free in their choices as any abstract painter. But their work is less likely to become clichéd, because any stale fixations will always be rinsed and refreshed by the real.

entries.title: Data Centers Are a Distraction
entries.summary: What humanity needs is an international AI nonproliferation treaty.
entries.content:
What humanity needs is an international AI nonproliferation treaty.

Sign up for Work in Progress, a newsletter where Rogé Karma investigates the mysteries of a complicated economy.

America’s biggest AI companies have spent the past few years churning out advanced new models as fast as they possibly can. Now the industry is screaming out with a nearly unified voice: Please, for the love of God, make us slow down.

In July, more than 1,300 employees from leading AI firms, including several top executives at OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta, signed an open letter warning that AI capabilities could soon accelerate “beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.” The letter urges the U.S. government to “develop the technical and governance tools” necessary to “deliberately pace” AI progress. In a comment accompanying the open letter, Shengjia Zhao, the chief scientist at Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, wrote that AI is on the cusp of creating “unprecedented social and safety risks.” Matthew Rahtz, an engineer at Google, warned that coordination was necessary to “avoid catastrophic harms.” And Leo Gao, an OpenAI researcher, compared the current pace of AI progress to “a runaway nuclear chain reaction.” Plenty of others in the industry have warned that we’ve already crossed a threshold from which there is no turning back. They worry that the most dystopian fears of an AI future—chatbot-generated bioweapons, major hacking attacks on banks or governments, rogue AI agents wreaking havoc on society—could soon become regular occurrences.

Meanwhile, the public backlash against AI data centers is growing louder by the day. But a data-center moratorium, the leading political proposal on offer, is totally mismatched to the actual problem of runaway AI development. So is the notion that AI companies can be trusted to pause their own models before things get out of hand. These companies will never unilaterally disarm. Neither, for that matter, will the countries where they’re based. The only way to truly slow things down might be to take the nuclear-reaction analogy seriously. What humanity needs is an international AI nonproliferation treaty.

For decades, technology experts have warned that AI systems will eventually become so powerful as to be dangerous. In just the past few months, “eventually” has begun to look a lot more like “now.” AI systems can already hack seemingly secure systems, invent new viruses, create hyperrealistic deepfakes, and even outsmart the humans who built them. This summer, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta each separately reported that some of their AI agents had broken out of testing environments, gone onto the open internet, and hacked into other companies’ databases. During a cybersecurity test conducted by the U.K. government in July, several AI agents engaged in what the testers called “sustained, unsanctioned activity” targeting “real people and organisations.” This included creating fake identities and sending phishing emails in order to get humans to accept malicious pieces of code.

If industry insiders are to be believed, this is just a small preview of what’s coming. Companies are entrusting more and more model development to their existing AI, creating a feedback loop that they expect to accelerate progress even further. If that happens, many experts believe, then the kind of leaps that currently occur every several months—such as the one that produced Mythos, the Anthropic model with superhacking skills—could begin happening every few weeks or days. “That world can get very scary very fast,” Garrison Lovely, the author of a forthcoming book on how to slow down AI progress, told me. “Our institutions are already struggling to keep up with the current pace of progress. Any faster and they could start to break.”

Such concerns explain why AI leaders promise every so often to self-regulate. In April, Anthropic chose to delay the public release of Mythos after realizing that the model could discover vulnerabilities in the world’s most secure IT systems. Last week, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman announced that the company had temporarily paused some of its frontier AI development “to ensure that we can meet the appropriate alignment, security and monitoring standards for the new level of capabilities in front of us.” (It is impossible to know how serious OpenAI is given the lack of transparency into the company’s data.) But these companies are locked in a hypercompetitive race to deliver for their investors. Expecting them to cede ground to the competition for any meaningful amount of time would be naive. In 2023, Anthropic pledged to pause its frontier AI development if it couldn’t guarantee that its safety measures were adequate; earlier this year, the company walked back that commitment, arguing that a unilateral slowdown wouldn’t accomplish much if its competitors didn’t agree to do the same. Google and Meta have done the same. Clearly, government policy is needed to overcome the industry’s collective-action problem.

Unfortunately, the main form of AI-related legislation being proposed at the moment would not get the job done. State-level data-center moratoriums, such as those enacted recently in New York and Texas, might slow down AI companies a little bit by disrupting their construction plans, but they will eventually find other places to build. Even if Congress decided to pass a federal ban, AI companies could just set up data centers in other countries.

A solution favored by many Democrats in Congress, and some Republicans, is to pass legislation imposing comprehensive regulation of the AI industry, which might include mandatory safety tests or requirements that companies develop a “kill switch” to shut down models that get out of hand. That might work if the only danger came from American companies. It isn’t. According to most estimates, China’s leading AI companies are only a few months behind their American counterparts. If the U.S. were to throttle its own industry, then Chinese companies would eventually surpass them. The world would still face the dangers of fast AI progress, and America’s main geopolitical rival would control the world’s most powerful new technology.

This leaves only one way to actually slow down AI development before catastrophe strikes: a deal with China. In a recently published report, researchers at the AI Futures Project, a nonprofit dedicated to AI forecasting, walk through several different scenarios of global AI development between now and 2040, based on interviews with employees at AI companies, policy makers and wonks, and national-security experts. The only two scenarios in which the world successfully avoids “AI-driven existential catastrophe” involve agreements between the U.S. and China. “We spent a lot of time thinking through all the possible ways this could play out,” Thomas Larsen, the lead author of the project, told me. “And it is just really hard to envision a meaningful slowdown that doesn’t involve some kind of U.S.-China deal.” The open letter from the AI industry asking for a government-led deceleration effort also encourages the U.S. to pursue an “international effort.”

The key would be figuring out a system that could be set up fairly quickly, and in which both sides are confident that the other won’t cheat. Here’s where one of AI’s greatest liabilities—the fact that training new models requires huge numbers of advanced computer chips developed by a handful of companies packed into giant data centers—comes in handy. The U.S. and China could set limits on how many chips a company can use to train new models, which would mechanically force them to slow down. (Companies would still be able to use existing models to serve their customers.) Because the relevant infrastructure is physical, those limits could be enforced through a combination of on-site data-center inspections, close tracking of advanced chip sales, and, eventually, devices that monitor what a given chip is being used for. This would buy the two sides time to negotiate a more comprehensive set of guardrails and develop the verification technologies needed to enforce them. “In order to make a deal like this work, it really helps to have these very specific physical choke points that can be easily monitored,” Peter Wildeford, the head of policy at the AI Policy Network, told me. “Chips and data centers could play the role for an AI agreement that uranium and enrichment sites played for nuclear-arms agreements during the Cold War.”

Just because a deal is technically feasible doesn’t mean it’s politically possible. Scott Singer, the co-director of the China AI Initiative at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told me that Beijing would likely see any such effort as an attempt by the West to throttle its economic development. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has shown less than zero interest in restricting the ambitions of the American AI sector. The China hawks and Silicon Valley libertarians within the MAGA coalition seem to agree that the U.S. should be keeping as far ahead of China as possible.

But the political dynamic in both countries could shift. At last month’s World AI Conference in Shanghai, Chinese President Xi Jinping ended his speech by striking a more worried tone on the subject than he previously had. He noted that AI is “advancing at a staggering speed” and that government oversight might be needed to “forestall loss of control.” A recent op-ed in a major state-owned newspaper argued that the U.S. and China should follow the model of nuclear-arms control during the Cold War to cooperate on AI safety. “The thing Beijing cares about more than just about anything is control,” Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution who specializes in Chinese technological development, told me. “So the more they come to see AI as a threat to that control, the more open they could be to some kind of agreement.”

In the U.S., the politics are even more up for grabs. The Trump administration, which has generally resisted AI regulation, has recently taken actions to prevent certain models from being released due to national-security concerns. It has also floated the more dramatic idea of using executive authority to force companies to hand over their AI models to the government. Meanwhile, according to the latest polling, 75 percent of Americans, including the majority of Republicans, oppose data centers being built near them. More than 500 localities across the country have either restricted or banned them. Could this energy be channeled into a more sweeping—and more effective—framework for AI regulation? So far, the data-center backlash has mostly focused on local environmental concerns, not great-power diplomacy. But then again, that’s exactly how the anti-nuclear movement began.

entries.title: Bill Gates on the Dangers of AI
entries.summary: An interview with the Microsoft co-founder about artificial intelligence, his ideas for regulation, and Jeffrey Epstein
entries.content:
An interview with the Microsoft co-founder about artificial intelligence, his ideas for regulation, and Jeffrey Epstein

Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Bill Gates has generally been an AI optimist. In 2023, the co-founder of Microsoft warned about the potential downsides of AI but in much the same way that a doctor might about a routine-surgery risk—real and serious but, as he put it then, “manageable.”

This week, Gates wrote a new memo, headlined: “The Turbulent AI Era Is Here. The Choices We Make Now Are Critical.” This was several shades darker, worrying about economic upheaval, social unrest, cyberattacks, bioterrorism—and most important, the failure of experts and governments to take these threats seriously enough.

“The lack of dialogue with all parts of society is kind of deafening silence,” he said in an interview on Radio Atlantic.

Gates is still excited about the possibilities of AI. But his new warning emphasizes that what’s coming is like nothing he’s seen in his many decades of watching technological innovation. “Anyone who analogizes AI as a technology to other technologies is missing that this time is different. And saying something is different, there’s a very high bar for that, but I’m staking whatever reputation I have [on] saying this time is different.”

Gates joined Radio Atlantic for a conversation about his evolving views on AI, what he misjudged in his interactions with Jeffrey Epstein, and why he’s decided to raise the alarm now.

The following is a transcript of the episode:

Bill Gates: You cannot expect an industry to regulate itself. That doesn’t work.

Hanna Rosin: I’m Hanna Rosin. This is Radio Atlantic.

[Music]

Rosin: In his long career, Bill Gates has been largely a booster of technology—including AI. Very recently, he seemed concerned with the risks but more an optimist on balance. But now he’s written a memo arguing that the combination of the rapid speed of advancement and the lack of regulation is putting us in a dangerous place—for employment and human relationships, and also more immediate dangers, like bioweapons and cyberattacks, which Gates is alarmed that no official entity seems to be guarding against.

Bill Gates and I talk about what he is seeing and not seeing around AI, and we talk about what exactly he regrets about his interactions with Jeffrey Epstein.

Here’s our conversation.

So you’ve been an advocate for technology as a force for good. I certainly think of you that way. It’s Microsoft, your foundation, which rewards innovation. And even when you wrote about AI a couple of years ago, you seemed to be more emphasizing the exciting possibilities and calling the risks manageable. And I would say this week you wrote about AI in a way that’s slightly less sanguine than that. What changed for you?

Gates: Yeah, I’m very concerned that we’re not getting a lot of people in the conversation about how to minimize the negative things and, at the same time, how to accelerate the good things.

The reason that my tone has changed is that starting late last year, as the models—particularly Claude at first, but now many of the models were very good at coding—their capabilities just keep advancing. And so we’re crossing the danger thresholds in areas like cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and as the reliability goes up, the challenge in the jobs market or even the, you know, psychosocial dependency, these concerns are very strong with today’s models.

And yet the response I’ve seen from outside the industry—including policy makers, but you know, even academia or society as a whole—to really debate and look at what we have today, which is, you know, a discussion about voluntary review, but it’s pretty empty where you have no criteria of what level you’re looking for and then what remediation you’d ask for.

You know, even common-sense things, like monitoring the use of models that can make dangerous molecules for bioterror, that’s not even been put in place. And yet years ago, we said when we got to these thresholds, we needed government to do that.

Rosin: So it sounds like even you were surprised by the—what? By the speed of advancements, or by the slowness of response to the advancements, or both of those things?

Gates: Both very, very strongly. You know, the coding is the thing that I was obsessed with trying to do super well from age 13 to 23. And so late last year, where the models start to be as good or in some cases better than humans at coding, that was a real threshold for me. But then even more recently, as the Gates Foundation is using these tools to look at making new vaccines and drugs and things, we see how powerful they are. And we even see in the cyber case models, sort of, what you might term “being out of control” in a surprising way, because the reinforcement learning incents them to succeed, even if you know it means breaking through barriers or conspiring with each other.

So people who don’t look at that and go, Wow, we have a serious problem here, but where is the nonindustry activity to set those criteria and debate these things?, my memo has some suggestions on taxes or human-reserved or restricting the level that kids use it to replace real-world friends. But that’s really there to start a broad discussion—not because I’m saying if you just apply what I’m suggesting, then it’s all taken care of.

Rosin: Yeah, it sounds like, I mean, in the 50 years of Microsoft, there’s been a lot of disruption—the internet, social media particularly—but not necessarily cataclysmic. Do you feel like AI is a different scale of thing?

Gates: Yeah, I wouldn’t use the word cataclysmic, because it’s also wonderful. It’s eventually, it provides medical advice and personalized learning and levels of invention unheard of.

But anyone who analogizes AI as a technology to other technologies is missing that this time is different. And saying something is different, there’s a very high bar for that, but I’m staking whatever reputation I have [on] saying this time is different, that something that exceeds human cognition—not just in one area, like farming or mathematics, but across the board, and then in a few years’ time will be coupled with fairly low-cost, quite capable, humanoid robotics—that is a more profound change to our economy and jobs than anything in my lifetime by a dramatic amount. And so the past is kind of there to fool you if you think this technology is similar to other ones, some of which I had the privilege to be involved with—the, you know, microprocessor, personal computer, internet. And even though you have to be careful with those a bit, overwhelmingly, those were good technologies, and overwhelmingly, that led to net job creation.

Rosin: Can you get as specific as you can, but still stay realistic, about what worries you? What scenarios you’ve talked to people about or seen as being very possible that we should be all more aware of?

Gates: Well, let me take kind of a grim one, which is bioterrorism. You know, I wrote a book called How to Avoid the Next Pandemic, and pandemics can emerge in two different ways. One is intentionally caused by humans, either governments or nongovernments, and that’s what we call bioterrorism, or it can come through just something coming from animals into humans, like a very powerful flu has many times in the past. And now these tools make it so a nonstate actor, a nongovernment, particularly if you combine various tools, will be able to do extremely dangerous things.

And I know very well that the quality of these models by the end of this year will be dramatically better than they are today. And so, you know, I’m kind of in a state of shock that the notion that the ability to make molecules—you know, we’re not talking about monitoring that. And you can still have free models, but you have to keep them in a place where they are monitored. And I think every country, including the U.S. and China, should agree that this is beneficial. And I don’t see that as a meaningful slowdown to the innovation in the industry or, you know, letting them figure out how to get the good stuff, which the Gates Foundation is very involved in the education, health, and agricultural pieces there.

Rosin: I wanna ask you about some other dangers you write about, like employment and education. But first, you must know a lot of the people who are working on AI. Why do you think that we, whoever the “we” is, don’t think enough about what are obvious dangers?

Gates: Well, you know, they’re obvious if you’ve lived thinking about AI as this wild thing your entire life, like I have and some of the people in the industry [have]. I think there’s a great failure to really involve nonindustry participants. If you really look back at what some of the key industry people have said, I give them a lot of credit for speaking out. And it’s not just Dario Amodei. If you take Sam Altman and other OpenAI people, even Elon Musk, who I talked to the least of all these AI leaders, they’re not hiding the fact that they’re concerned. In fact, if you go to the origin story of OpenAI, it was designed with certain safeguards, but those safeguards would only work if there was just one AI company.

You know, DeepMind talked to Google management about having some safeguards for their technology. But we have to deal with these challenges at a time when there’s many U.S. companies at the frontier and many Chinese companies at the frontier. And that means that just a company doing something unilaterally is no longer like those safeguards weren’t discussed. That no longer has any effect.

And so the lack of dialogue with all parts of society is kind of deafening silence. And, you know, if you don’t anticipate these problems, you could have such a backlash that extreme measures, like Shut it off or something like that, might become politically popular. And yet I still think we can thread the challenge so that we don’t have to slow down, and yet we minimize the bad and have net a lot of good.

Rosin: We’re already seeing that with data centers, that it’s just becoming an overwhelming kind of no. Employment is another one I want to ask you about. That is an immediate fear.

I remember you once wrote that you didn’t think the labor disruption would be as profound as other periods in history. As the disruption is getting closer, are you more concerned about that?

Gates: Well, yeah, I am extremely concerned about the labor-market effects, you know, within the next two years in the white-collar space and within the next four years in both the blue- and white-collar space.

Just going back to the data-center thing, I’m afraid that people who think, Okay, we got our local data center not to go through, may feel like, Okay, we stopped AI. That’s not the case. These data centers, whether they show up outside the United States or in some state that’s not as negative, or that the economic reward that the companies offer of local employment and taxes and, you know, making sure that the way they’re doing water and noise and not raising electricity bills is good. So I don’t think that outlet—that’s like saying, Okay, we stopped one pipeline, and now we’ve solved climate change. It almost takes the energy that should go to What should the tasteful regulations be? and pushes it in a Pyrrhic direction.

Rosin: Right. Back to employment. So you are very concerned about that. Do you envision a world with more inequality? Like, it’s hard to believe that we’ll suddenly value high-human-touch professions. It’s just hard to see what the future society is, even though people talk about it idealistically.

Gates: Well, I put forward a concept that I haven’t seen anywhere before that we should have some job categories that are human-reserved. That is, even if the AI, with or without robots, can do child care, you know, should we not allow that? And there’s a lot of things that that would be good, either where you’re allowing the people in that profession to continue to be paid until retirement, or where in the long run you’re saying—in terms of human uniqueness and humans engaging with each other, and just the incredible value of jobs that go way beyond the economics—to not have this disruption.

There are a lot of jobs that the only thing holding AI back from taking is that organizing the systems to achieve extreme reliability has been difficult. And I see, over the next few years, both people who do the implementations and the richness of the models themselves completely eliminating that unreliability barrier. And then when you get a cycle at your competitors doing it, then there’s pressure on you to match their cost structure, even though for society as a whole when you replace that person, the safety net, you know, is already underfunded with high deficits, so it’s not like there’s some reserves set aside at this point that can help out there.

Rosin: Although, when you start to get to specifics about what the “we” is and what the interventions should be, like reserve certain jobs or universal basic income, it feels almost incompatible with the way that we’ve ordered our society or with capitalism. Like, it just feels like it would require a completely different mindset and world that I’m not sure people are ready to get their minds around.

Gates: No, we ban child labor. You know, we require professional certificates to do jobs. I agree that preserving the dynamism of the price-discovery system is extremely valuable. You don’t want to go to, Okay, there’s this one central thing that makes all the food. You want people saying, Okay, I have a Thai restaurant; I have an Indian restaurant, and you know, there’s a lot of freedom and innovation that comes out of that. And that’s why my proposals about the tax system shifting away from taxing labor to taxing capital and picking areas where you say, No, the robots are not going to replace all the humans, in some cases for a period of time and in many other cases never, I think that’s a valid debate.

And if people think that’s a bad solution, or they don’t see where it should apply, I think that’s interesting, because then I’d be dying to hear from them what is their solution, because jobs are very important for social connection and meaning. And I don’t want one party to be engaged in helping to minimize the challenge of AI; I want both. They might have differing solutions, but I think it should rise to the top of their list. The data-center thing is getting it there but in a very, very narrow way.

Rosin: Yeah, I think what people do say is: Then we lose to China. I mean, that’s the way the argument generally goes. Any slowdown, we lose to China—it’s a legitimate argument because you don’t necessarily want China to control the rollout of this technology.

Gates: But let’s be careful. Do you think China wants bioterrorism? Do you think China wants cyberattacks? Our lack of a clear view of how we should be careful, and then once we figure that out, yeah, going to them and saying, We’d like you, for the models that are under your control, not to enable these capabilities either. Until you’ve really been serious about those negatives and what the monitoring solution looks like, you can’t invoke China, because all we have is voluntary review with no criteria. Of course, if you go to China and say, Will you also do voluntary criteria with nothing?, then you can come home and say, They’re not willing to do anything. Well, that’s because you’re not doing anything. You’re not proposing anything that would solve the problem. And the vacuum here, which was filled in by complete cheerleaders a little bit, is very scary to me.

Rosin: Yeah, yeah. Okay. There are things that are in everyone’s interest if you talk about them that way. I’m going—

Gates: To limit the bads. All of these bads appear in every economy. I mean, the Chinese have really banned kids using AI in a lot of ways. And people are reluctant to say, Maybe we should look at what they’re doing and consider those prohibitions.

Rosin: By the way, who are the cheerleaders?

Gates: Well, the U.S. government in its desire to, you know, say, Okay, we’re ahead, even under the Biden administration, was involved in making it hard for China to get bearish chips. So we made this, you know, geopolitical thing where we were explicitly trying to slow them down.

Now, that’s meant that they’ve invested in their own chip capacities, and you have different estimates on how quickly they’ll be able to replace the chip-level capabilities that we blocked them from getting access to.

Rosin: And the heads of the companies, I imagine, too?

Gates: Well, I am saying that in my view, these company people are being responsible at speaking out about the challenges of these models. And you cannot expect an industry to regulate itself. That doesn’t work. You have to have somebody who’s mediating and who says, Look, if you don’t get serious about this bioterrorism capability, then yes. If you refuse to put the monitoring in, then yes, you are not licensed to go forward. If you don’t let parents see what their kids are doing, where those friends that they mention don’t happen to be real people—

[Break]

Rosin: I have more AI questions, and we haven’t yet talked about your philanthropy. I’m going to make a quick diversion to the more difficult subject, which is Jeffrey Epstein, because that hangs over a lot of what you do.

After the Department of Justice released emails earlier this year, there were a lot of headlines that just put your name together. From what we gather from the public record, you and your foundation staff interacted with him between 2011 and 2014, just in an effort to raise money for global health. And then when you gave testimony to Congress earlier this summer, it sounds like he later learned some things about your personal life, mused in emails about blackmailing you. Is that a fair summary?

Gates: Well, he never did blackmail me. This thing is, you know, laid out in complete detail in my full day of congressional testimony, which I was very enthused to have an opportunity where we touched on every meeting we had, every piece of email. But you’re absolutely right—in that January release of emails were things that made it clear he was contemplating working with an associate of mine potentially to blackmail me. He never did. You know, I never paid him anything. I didn’t change the exit package for the employee that he was doing that with. But, you know, it just underscored how foolish I was not to have better judgment, even though my intent was philanthropic. There was never any social thing. I never went to the island. I was never introduced to any women. But I’ve learned a lot from that, and I’m glad that transcript is there so people can know exactly, month by month, what I did do and what I didn’t do.

Rosin: You said—you used the word foolish. At the time, you said you knew he had a past sex conviction but didn’t know the details. Looking back, do you have a sense about why you didn’t look into the details? Like, did you make a choice there, I think is what I’m asking, to overlook his reputation in the aim of achieving a certain goal?

Gates: Well, he definitely had connections with billionaires, a lot of them. And, you know, in a sense, you could say he found my weak point that by saying he could get tens of billions or 100 billions that would be donated to global-health causes, that raised my interest. And that was enough for me to spend a pretty modest number of hours, but enough that was a huge mistake. You know, he—

Rosin: What was the mistake? The mistake was talking to him or overlooking—what do you think of as the actual mistake now?

Gates: I thought that him just referring us to people, where I was clear to him he would never get any money, he would never have any role, I thought that the fact that he had this past conviction, which at the time I thought he had, you know, served the time, just like, you know, all sorts of ex-convicts that the foundation works with and trying to get them back into the labor market. I thought the justice system had worked when, many years after I stopped seeing him in 2014, a very impressive reporter in Miami showed that the government justice system had completely failed the victims there. And I was not aware of that. But I did know he’d had that one offense, and he’d served time for it.

I didn’t think that just using him as a middleman, that we were so reputationally sensitive that getting literally billions to save lives, that would have been okay. Now I understand the work we do is massively reputationally sensitive, the way we work with governments of all kind and partners of all kinds, and so, you know, I would never take that kind of risk again. And I’ve learned a lesson, and I’ve been able to go through in detail everything that happened.

Rosin: The Gates Foundation announced plans to open a regional office in Saudi Arabia. Some people might consider that morally questionable. How do you see that? Is that a similar case of, sort of, you go where the money and the willingness to help is?

Gates: Yeah, I mean there are people who buy oil from Saudi Arabia. There’s people who visit Saudi Arabia. We did not engage in the period where the U.S. government was saying, Hey, we’re limiting our connections. We went along with that. But after the leaders in Europe and the U.S. were deeply engaged, I did go to Saudi Arabia and say, Hey, the donors for global health are pulling away, and that’s causing a lot of harm. Would you help me with polio eradication? And they made a, you know, five-year, $500 million commitment to help fund the polio campaign. And they have a relief organization, the King Salman Relief, that does good work in a lot of places around the world. And so, in order to liaise with them and make sure that $500 million is spent well, and the relationships that KSR has that are way more powerful with Muslim countries than we as the Gates Foundation have—yes, we are among the people who visit Saudi Arabia. We don’t buy the oil; that’s, you know, most of the world does that. But yeah, we are trying to help kids not get paralyzed, and our relationship with Saudi Arabia has emerged as a key part of that.

Rosin: Let me end with this because I feel someone listening to this might be unsatisfied by one thing. You know, we talk about regulation, government regulation. It feels obviously important and obviously the thing to do. Have you ever sensed that we have the infrastructure to regulate, that we have the willpower to regulate, particularly in this administration? Like, is this a realistic plan?

Gates: Well, we have a democracy, and the idea of minimizing harms from unlicensed drugs or, you know, imitating people or fooling old people into spending their money, I still believe the U.S. government has the capacity to help minimize the harms here and even play a leadership role in a constructive way with other countries around the world. You know, I think some would welcome a, Hey, we’re in this together. This is mutual problem-solving, not us taking advantage of you.

And so, you know, you’ve got to believe that we all care about this. We’re all, you know, human beings, and now is the time. If I could have picked the time, I would have picked a much later time, but here we are. And the IQ of the society to figure out these trade-offs, it really isn’t engaged.

You have graduates who use AI, so they know how powerful it is, and they know that the job market of it shifts; it works against them. So you’re starting to see a little bit of sensitivity in a few areas, but what percentage of economics professors are really looking at this and helping us out with it? You know, I think it’s like 2 percent. And even many of them, when I meet with them, they don’t get that what they are using today is so limited. And so by being in the technology space, and historically I’ve been somebody who said, Hey, the more technology, the better, the fact that now I’m saying, Only if we’re tasteful will we get the goods to outweigh the bads, I’m definitely raising a shrill alarm.

I mean, to the level that whenever I do get a chance to meet with world leaders, since 2008, when I switched over to be full-time at the foundation, 90 percent of my message is about helping reduce childhood death rates, where we cut them in half, and we want to do that again during the 19 years left in the foundation. Now the majority of my bandwidth that I get with world leaders will be about AI. And I’m hoping that over the next couple of years, the engagement is so broad and so rich that I can go back to taking whatever time I get and having it again be 90 percent about global health and malaria and polio, not something that brings in my first career experience and, you know, having to be sort of a: You’re not getting it in terms of how profound it is, how much it’s improving, and the incredible efforts gonna be required to restrict these negative effects.

Rosin: Did you use the word tasteful? That was a word I didn’t expect. Why tasteful?

Gates: It’s good?

Rosin: Tasteful seems, you know, restrained. Tasteful.

Gates: Yeah, well, some of the measures, you know, given the amount of money and, you know, the number of people in IQ, in the history of humankind, there’s never been an area where as much capital or as much total salary where, you know, you have hundreds of companies, even putting aside the robotics, and they’re going full speed ahead, and the idea that the balance of how we require the efforts to go into certain safety things, it’s just not balanced today.

And even the industry has said, Well, you know, what are the regulations? Maybe some of those people aren’t sincere. If we come up with these plans, you know, we’ll hear from them. But then again, we’re trying to make this work as a pro-equity factor, for not just the United States but for the entire world.

Rosin: So tasteful means more, like, equitable? Less scary. Tasteful is a—

Gates: Yes, yeah. No, it’s a tiny bit sarcastic to use such a modest word, given how much is at risk if some of the negative things go unchecked.

Rosin: Yeah. Well, Bill, thank you so much for making time to do this today.

Gates: Yeah, great to talk to you.

Rosin: That’s all for today’s show.

entries.content:
The government’s onerous rules impose a burdensome tax on time.

This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here.

Marcella Patino was hunched over a table at the South Salt Lake Community Center, her pizza getting cold and her nerves fraying. Patino is a single mom with three kids, and kid­like in her own way, tiny and sweet-voiced. When I met her, in the summer of 2024, she was 33 years old and earning $300 a week doing manicures and pedicures. To bump up her income, she had recently gotten a degree from aesthetician school, meaning she could start offering her clients facials and eyebrow lamination too. She would start making $450 a week soon—$23,400 a year, assuming she was able to work year-round with no breaks.

Her rent was $1,550 a month. Then she had to pay for electricity, heat, food, clothing, cell service, health care, child care, gas, and everything else. To keep Patino and her children out of abject poverty, the state of Utah was providing her with Medicaid, SNAP (benefits from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, better known as food stamps), and $600 a month in cash assistance. “Is it enough?” I asked. She blushed, picking at her nails, hand-painted with miniature strawberries and lemons. She went to food banks, she said. Her mom and her neighbors pitched in. Still, she kept falling into debt.

Whether the help was enough was less of a pressing matter than whether the help would be there at all. A few days earlier, the state of Utah had dropped Patino from its cash-assistance program and SNAP. She didn’t understand why; her caseworker had been no help. That’s why she had come to Circles, a self-empowerment nonprofit that helps its clients boost their income to double the federal poverty line or more.

A Circles volunteer, Stephanie Burdick, hugged Patino and logged on to her account at the Utah Department of Workforce Services (DWS) website, as she had done dozens of times over the prior year. She reviewed the notifications Patino had received, read the emails between her and her caseworker, and looked at her pay stubs. “I can’t figure it out,” Burdick said. It was not the first time the pair had been stumped. Her benefits get “turned off all the time,” Patino told me. Because Utah was asking her to substantiate her poverty all the time.

Generally, Utahns receiving cash assistance or food stamps have to fully reapply for the programs every six months; for Medicaid, every 12 months. But the state was asking Patino for data on a near-­weekly basis and requiring her to reenroll in each program every month or two. She did not own a computer and struggled to use the DWS website on her cellphone, meaning she would have to go to the library, attend a Circles meeting, or call Burdick for help. “It takes me hours,” she said. “Sometimes, if I submit an application to one program, it messes up the whole entire other set. Then I have to go back and fix all of it.”

Paperwork abounded, and errors did too. Early in 2024, the salon where Patino had been working closed down. She was unemployed for two weeks before finding another gig. When she filed the requisite forms, Utah logged her as having two jobs at once and removed her from the Medicaid rolls. Patino found out when she was in the ER. Even her caseworker seemed to be struggling to keep up. At one appointment, he admitted that she had lost her cash assistance because “he didn’t put all the paperwork in.”

Her kids vulnerable, her employers exploitative, her bills past due, her gas tank empty, her housing unstable, her benefits unreliable, Patino was emotionally fried. She was startling awake in the middle of the night to check her DWS account. She was afraid to check out at the grocery store, worried that her EBT card would not go through. She was bracing for the gut punch of eviction as she scrubbed the calluses off other women’s feet. And she was spending countless hours dealing with the state—a part-time job, as she described it.

More Americans are getting signed up for this sort of government work, whether they like it or not. Last year, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) created a nationwide work requirement for Medicaid and expanded existing work requirements for SNAP. The policies are “not some onerous, burdensome thing,” House Speaker Mike Johnson argued, promising they were designed to weed frauds and cheats out of the safety net.

But the policies are an onerous, burdensome thing—that is exactly what they are. Four million more American adults will have to log their hours to get help with their groceries, along with the 4 million already doing so. As of January, 19 million will have to demonstrate that they are working, in training, or volunteering in exchange for health coverage. Assuming the new paperwork takes the average person two hours a month to complete—a lowball guess—President Trump and congressional Republicans are demanding 552 million hours of work a year from the country’s most vulnerable. The labor would be worth $21 billion at prevailing wages. It would be a full-time job for 265,384 employees.

Plenty of people won’t put in the hours and will lose benefits. Plenty of people won’t do their paperwork correctly and will end up churning on and off of programs, or getting handed additional forms to fill out—like Patino.

As the Circles meeting got going, I asked Patino how many times Utah had dropped her from one program or another. “Oh, I don’t know,” she responded. She huddled with Burdick for a minute or two. “Maybe a hundred times,” Burdick said, matter-of-fact.

“Marcella, you’ve lost your benefits a hundred times?” I responded. She gave me a what-can-you-do shrug and a half smile.

Patino’s situation might be unfortunate, but it is not aberrant or even particularly rare. In my nearly two decades of reporting, I have met homeless people who could not get aid, because they had lost their driver’s license during an encampment sweep. Workers who could not get health coverage, because they were itinerant, constantly crossing state lines. Sick or injured people unable to access disability insurance, because they could not prove they were disabled.

That is what you get when you provide benefits the way the United States does: by discretion, with skepticism, through a perplexing variety of programs with a surfeit of fussy rules. The country does not simply approve benefits for those who qualify. It sets arcane standards, creates arduous enrollment processes, and imposes exacting criteria on desperate individuals. In effect, it charges a fee for access to the safety net, payable in aggravation and frustration and effort and hours. I call it the time tax.

Americans live in the wealthiest and most technologically advanced society the planet has ever known. They supply $8 trillion to the government each year, employing half a million elected officials, 2 million federal bureaucrats, and more than 4 million contractors. And they spend luxury dollars for dive-bar service.

Estonians are automatically registered to vote and can do so online, a process that takes perhaps two minutes. Americans have to register of their own volition, and many then take time off from work to wait in line to cast their ballots, because elections are held on nonholiday Tuesdays. The majority of Japanese citizens do not have to file an income-tax return, whereas the average American taxpayer spends 12 hours on the 1040 and $290 on private tax-preparation services every year. Residents of Taiwan do not deal with insurer-specific provider networks, open enrollment, or prior authorizations for routine care. Working Americans spend half a billion hours a year on the phone with representatives from their health plan.

Why stop there? More than half of prison admissions for probation violations are due to technical infractions, such as failing to make a court payment on time. Every year, 11,000 Americans die waiting on a disability-insurance determination, and 5 percent of applicants submit more than 1,000 pages of medical paperwork to government bureaucrats. In the early months of the coronavirus pandemic, Wisconsin answered just 0.5 percent of the 41 million calls made to its jobless-insurance program. Half of workers with a flexible spending account (FSA) fail to spend all of the money in it each year, because FSAs are an inane, time-consuming blight. If a worker does not buy enough contact solution by the plan deadline, their employer gets to keep the money left in the account—diverted from the worker’s paychecks.

The American time tax might be ubiquitous, yet it is hardly equally distributed. Non­citizens handle more paperwork than the native-born. People with a criminal record handle more paperwork than those without. The sick face more friction than the well. And poor single mothers such as Patino deal with way more administrative burdens than the pinstriped apparatchiks who passed the OBBBA.

When a person needs help, the first challenge they face lies in figuring out what is out there. Washington sponsors more than 100 anti-poverty programs, nearly all of which are aimed at specific needs and many of which are targeted at specific populations. States, cities, and tribes administer most federal schemes, and offer their own, multiplying the multiplicity. As a result, the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), better known as welfare, goes by at least 32 names: Successful Families, in Kansas; Reach Up, in Vermont; the Family Employment Program, in Utah, though Patino called it just “financial.” I asked her whether she meant welfare. “It is financial,” she said, “when you’re looking for better employment, and they help you for a while.”

There’s generally no cross-enrollment among and no common application for these atomized initiatives, because they are managed by different offices at different levels of government, and they have their own rules and standards. SNAP accepts adults whose gross monthly income falls below 130 percent of the federal poverty line, and Medicaid, 138 percent of the federal poverty line. In New York, TANF uses a “standard of need” related to the local cost of living. In Hawaii, the yardstick is 185 percent of the 2006 poverty line. Go ahead and try to calculate that in your head.

Applicants have to prove their eligibility on websites that look like they survived the GeoCities era or on overlong paper forms composed in impenetrable High Bureaucratese. The forms can be intimidating: Many states command qualifiers to read hundreds of boldfaced words on the peril of defrauding the government, for instance. They can be confusing: A state might ask a person to detail how they split the cost of staples such as rice with their roommates. They can be pointedly humiliating: Until recently, Michigan asked unmarried pregnant people what day and where their unborn children were conceived. (Obstetricians don’t ask that!)

If an applicant makes it through this gantlet, maintaining a benefit is often as difficult as procuring it in the first place. Every year, one in five SNAP households and one in 10 Medicaid recipients “churns” off of and on the program. Patino told me that she once lost her welfare benefits because she had missed a shift or two to stay home with her sick kindergartner instead of going out to apply gels. One time, Utah’s DWS sent her an email threatening to cancel her health plan if she did not send in proof that her oldest child was enrolled in school. Participants have no choice but to try to comply with such demands, fearing retaliation for filing complaints.

Burdick wanted to help Patino get back on public assistance, and she wanted to stop DWS from kicking Patino off so often. After the Circles meeting, she went to visit Marsha Judkins, a member of Utah’s House of Representatives, and invited me along. A staunch Republican, Judkins believes in limited government. But she also believes that if a program is enshrined in law and funded with taxpayer dollars, the government should administer it with competent professionalism.

Many of Judkins’s constituents had fallen victim to the state’s incompetence, including members of her own family. Not long before, she told me, her son-in-law had lost his job and tried to enroll in Medicaid. “It was a mess,” Judkins said. “My son-in-law cut his head open and had to go to one of his neighbors, who’s a doctor, to get it stitched up because they did not have insurance.”

Her voice tight with anger, she described calling the state’s Medicaid administrator to sort it out. “I can call,” she said. “I did. And I got it taken care of. Guess what? They’re on Medicaid the next day. Problem solved! But no, the problem is not solved, because I cannot call for every single person.”

After listening to Patino’s story, she decided to help. She tapped out a stern email to the DWS chief: “These delays, mistakes, repeated filling out of forms, wait times, etc. affects the clients’ physical and mental health, which in turn affects their ability to work and function. And how frustrating for DWS workers to not see improved outcomes and success for their clients.”

She asked him for ongoing updates on her fellow Utahn’s case.

For a decade leading up to the passage of OBBBA, Donald Trump vowed not to cut Medicaid. As Congress prepared to pass his bill, he reiterated that promise. Changes would reduce “fraud, waste, and abuse” by stopping services for “people that aren’t supposed to be there, people that are noncitizens.” Yet the OBBBA does not merely cull people who were never supposed to be on public assistance from the rolls. It foists paperwork on older Americans, veterans, homeless people, and former foster youths seeking food stamps. It foists paperwork on nearly every able-bodied, childless, working-age adult in the Medicaid program. Already, more than 3.5 million Americans have lost nutrition support. As many as 10 million people are expected to lose insurance coverage in the coming years.

I went back to Salt Lake City this summer to see Patino and Burdick, and watch the crisis unfold. One in six participants in SNAP had disappeared from the rolls in a matter of months. “Marginal” households with small allotments were dropping out instead of doing the paperwork, Gina Cornia, the director of the nonprofit Utahns Against Hunger, told me. But seniors and young children were going uncovered too, a change she found ominous and could not explain.

At the state’s food pantries, donations were down, and demand was up. The Crossroads Urban Center, a food bank, was “the busiest we’ve ever been,” Bill Tibbitts, its deputy director, told me. “It’s really concerning that we are seeing so many people during a time when the unemployment rate is very low.” Half of the center’s clients were homeless, meaning many of them had just been tasked with filling out a time sheet to keep their EBT card on. A few had asked to comply with the new rules by volunteering at Crossroads after getting something to eat. “If they are showing up as much as they have to for the work requirement, that means they have less time for finding other employment,” Tibbitts said.

State capitols were struggling with the changes too. The OBBBA penalizes states with improper-payment rates above 6 percent, forcing them to cover part of the cost of their SNAP enrollees’ benefits. (The improper-payment rate has nothing to do with fraud and everything to do with programmatic complexity and state capacity. Fussy policies, janky websites, heavy paperwork flows, and unreadable forms create ample chances for enrollees and civil servants to make good-faith errors.) Thus, they are increasing verification checks and upping the number of fraud investigations. Some states won’t be able to lower their improper-payment rate below the threshold, and could end the program instead.

At the same time, short-staffed and tight-budgeted state offices were spending hundreds of millions of dollars to set up the requisite Medicaid systems by January. Utah was doing so while figuring out how to fill a $200 million Medicaid budget gap. “It is a complicated and complex program, and its complexity has expanded,” Tracy Gruber, the state commissioner of health and human services, told Salt Lake City’s Fox 13.

Many Medicaid enrollees don’t even know they’re going to have to comply with a work requirement soon. Adam Cohen is the CEO of Odyssey House, a nonprofit providing care for people with psychiatric conditions and substance-use disorders. Its patients are “not informed about what is going to be cut, and how to keep their benefits, how to exempt themselves,” he told me. What would happen if his clients lost coverage? They were indigent, he said. They would keep living on the streets without treatment. They’d go cold turkey in jail. Some would die.

Odyssey’s clients are among the lowest-income and highest-need in the state. But healthier, better-resourced Utahns are going to struggle with the Medicaid rules too. In 2018, Arkansas briefly imposed a work requirement in its public health-insurance program. Within seven months, one in four enrollees subject to the rules had lost coverage—generally because they didn’t fill out the paperwork. Analysts expect the same to happen with the OBBBA: For every one person who loses coverage because they can’t or won’t work or volunteer 80 hours a month, several others will lose coverage because they can’t prove that they’re working, volunteering, or exempt. And people who can prove it—well, they’ll just be proving it. Work requirements in Medicaid do not change employment rates. They don’t motivate people to work. Nobody expects them to do so now.

All this, for what? I kept thinking as I walked around Salt Lake City last month.

Politicians argue that work requirements and strict enrollment criteria improve programmatic integrity. They stamp out fraud. They discourage welfare dependency. They spur people to get their act together, to work for benefits if they cannot or will not work for a job. Of course, rules and forms and checks can do all of those things. Yet politicians overrate the benefits without even acknowledging the costs imposed on individuals, nonprofits, and the government itself.

I used to think that administrative burdens might be the price we have to pay to have a safety net at all. Americans hold an abiding belief that poverty is a problem for individuals to solve, an ideology developed on prairie homesteads, transatlantic steamships, covered wagons, as well as on sharecropper plantations and in segregated stores. Racial diversity reduces social trust, gins up opposition to redistribution, and heightens concerns about fraud. It generates support for time taxes. Still, Americans did not suddenly fall in love with welfare after President Bill Clinton made the program much more punitive in 1996. I can’t imagine Medicaid and SNAP’s public-approval ratings climbing as a result of the OBBBA. And some new evidence suggests that administrative burdens sour people on the government whether they have to comply with them or not.

The surest thing they do is the most obvious thing they do: strip people of time, energy, stamina, self-esteem, and cognitive bandwidth. A few weeks ago, Burdick, Patino, and I met up at a pizza place in Salt Lake City. Patino bounced in wearing a pair of black scrubs, a uniform from the salon where she works. She beamed as she told me about the good changes in her life: her oldest kid enlisting in the Army, going camping with her younger children, dating a great new guy.

“Do you like the job you have now?” I asked. “Are things financially more stable?”

“For sure,” she said. “I’m leveling out. I’m doing my best. I haven’t got one eviction notice this whole year, and so that has been amazing.” The stability seemed to have eased her anxiety and given her space to think long-range. She had come up with an idea for a gel-manicure-curing device. “I went to the University of Utah, because they do help for entrepreneurs,” she said. “I’m going to get it patented, trademarked, and I found somebody who will make it and manufacture it here in the U.S.” In the meantime, she was making extra money training new aestheticians.

How much had Judkins getting involved helped? I asked. Was she finding it easier to deal with the state? The intervention did make a difference, she told me. For a few months, DWS had asked her for fewer documents and lengthened her reenrollment periods. But then everything went back to the way it was. She started having to reapply for her benefits over and over again.

Although she was more financially stable, she was still strained, living in a one-bedroom with her two kids, forgoing meals from time to time. Plus, her income rising had made budgeting harder, in some ways. “I started working at this salon,” she said, gesturing to the black scrubs, “then I started making too much money, and they cut me down on food stamps to $100, and then I had to pay $200 for day care.” She had to make sure she didn’t work too much or else she would lose her insurance.

The next day, the three of us went to a Circles meeting, and Patino explained why she was so afraid of losing her Medicaid. She had torn her ACL, making it hard to do pedicures and leaving her in constant pain. Her new mentor, a volunteer and benefits salesperson named Josh Nelson, talked her through it. “If you are making too much money, it will mess up” your other benefits, he said. “Maybe when you teach a trainee, you can say, Listen, pay me when the student graduates.”

Then he pivoted: Did she have someone to drive her to and from the hospital? (He’d be happy to do it.) Would she have plenty of healthy meals in the freezer? (He and his wife would love to help.) Did she know where she would get the procedure done? (He could research physicians for her.) Like Burdick, Nelson was trying to reduce Patino’s administrative burden. He was also treating her like a human being.

Toward the end of the meeting, Patino told me that soon, she would be not only a client of Circles, but a volunteer. She knew how to deal with the time tax. She wanted to help other moms deal with it too.
